And just to take us further out on the limb, we've never directly had a French Monarch although it's a common mistake. The Normans, yes, the Angevins, yes, but not the French (although there was a brief period of a few months when the French were technically ruling England and there have been plenty of marriages into the French monarchy).

Most of the place that we call France today wasn't even French until the Angevins totally lost the plot and lost all their lands (and heads), and it's the dual claim to those lands that has led to the whole centuries long antagonism over who had the 'true' right over lands on both sides of the channel.

I'll get my own coat, pipe, and slippers...

posts.name: Silverleaf
posts.cooked:
I'm yet to find anyone in my pedigree that wasn't born in England, but the furthest back I've gone is the 1730s. Some branches I've stalled out on in the mid 19th century due to extremely common names. Finding a John Roberts in a large town with a father called John Roberts when neither of them appear in the census I'm concerned with is IMPOSSIBLE.

So note to prospective/future parents: don't give your child a common name, especially if your surname is a common one. And don't for the love of genealogy name a child after a parent or an already-deceased sibling. Just don't.

posts.name: Mezike
posts.cooked:
My family tree is a total clustermess. One strand of the family basically goes back forever in the same few villages in Dorset, mostly farmers until the last century or so when they were mostly shopkeepers. The rest of it is a spaghetti heap of dead ends with Irish, French, Canadian, and a bunch of other influences including some who seem to have existed in the 19th century equivalent of being completely off the grid.

My kids will have it even harder as my wife's family aren't actually sure about their lineage beyond the last couple of generations, although it's highly likely that the family name came from a Russian soldier who went to Hungary and changed his name to something that sounded a little more Hungarian. Apparently it's a fairly unique surname that is not normal for Hungary but which is used in the Persian region, so there could be an even more convoluted backstory involving a Persian family migrating to Russia and then into Hungary. But there are still more complications that muddy the waters of this part of the story even further, and with so many public records lost, destroyed, or forged during the successive Nazi and Communist occupations nobody really has a scooby about their true geneology. We just like to say that we're starting the family anew from these existing generations

posts.name: arenson9
posts.cooked:
My grandfather's grandfather was apparently a well known Jewish leader of some type, at least in his region of the Pale of Settlement, earning the family name Kadushin, yiddish for Holy One.

When we were in Israel in 1982, we went to a Kibbutz where that same grandfather's cousin lived. My sister and I got to meet our 3rd cousins, though we couldn't talk to them much, since we only spoke English and they mostly only spoke Hebrew.

My grandmother, in her 80s, revealed in an interview that we have on tape, that she was 'a love child'. Her birth broke up two families. She had a lot of older half-siblings, many of whom resented her and treated her poorly. Her husband, my grandfather, grew up in an orphanage. He had many siblings in the orphanage, but said they were kinda just like everyone else, rather than feeling close. Due to both of them missing out on strong family ties growing up, they were both very focused on family and it has led to fairly strong bonds in their children, grandchildren, and greatgrandchildren.

My wife likes to tell the story of her family tumbleweed. When she was researching her genealogy, she started coming across a bunch of familiar names and realized that not too many generations back a couple of close cousins had married. In fact, she also tells the story of, I think her grandmother talking to her mother, saying something along the lines of, 'I wonder what life would be like if we'd stayed on the farm and you'd married your cousins, like everyone else.' That's rural eastern Kentucky for you.
